bug_description.normalized: The staged `fuzz_pkcs15_reader` witness is a little-endian uint16 length-prefixed smartcard APDU-response stream. Early `COOLKEY_INS_LIST_OBJECTS` replies materialize many placeholder `sc_cardctl_coolkey_object_t` entries, including repeated descriptors whose first 14 bytes decode to `object_id = 0x20202020` and `object_length = 0x202020ff`, plus additional distinct IDs such as `0x62f40600`; `coolkey_initialize()` truncates `0x202020ff` to `object_len = 8447` when building `priv->objects_list`. During PKCS#15 certificate matching, `coolkey_find_object_by_template()` reaches `coolkey_fill_object()` for a candidate whose cached `data` is still NULL and allocates 8447 bytes. The vulnerable source then executes `obj_entry = coolkey_find_object_by_id(&priv->objects_list, obj->id);`, but the registered SimCList comparator is inverted: `coolkey_compare_id()` returns `1` when two IDs are equal while `list_locate()` treats comparator result `0` as a match. The lookup can therefore return another non-matching list element. If that peer's `data` is also NULL, lines 1420-1421 store the same `new_obj_data` pointer in both list nodes. During `sc_disconnect_card()`, `coolkey_free_private_data()` frees `o->data` for every element in `priv->objects_list`, so the shared 8447-byte buffer is freed twice at `src/libopensc/card-coolkey.c:819`. AddressSanitizer reports both frees at that line and the allocation at `coolkey_fill_object` line 1401. The provided `patch.diff` adds a later duplicate-ID guard, but the exact staged source also contains the earlier comparator/list-lookup defect that directly creates the shared-pointer alias on this witness.

source.code: return coolkey_apdu_io(card, COOLKEY_CLASS, COOLKEY_INS_LIST_OBJECTS, seq, 0, NULL, 0, &rbuf, &rbuflen, NULL, 0);
source.description: First project-side materialization of attacker-controlled state on the crashing path: the LIST_OBJECTS APDU copies one fuzzed reader-response chunk into `object_info`, the structure later parsed into object IDs and lengths for `priv->objects_list`.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is consumed by `fuzz_pkcs15_reader` as a sequence of little-endian uint16 length-prefixed reader-response chunks. Parsing the saved file shows many early 18-byte chunks whose first 14 bytes are `20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 ff 20 20 20`, plus distinct descriptors such as `62 f4 06 00 20 20 7a ff 20 20 20 ff 20 20`; those exact bytes are what OpenSC reads into `object_info` here.
source.note: This is earlier than the later `bebytes2ulong` parses in `coolkey_initialize()`: it is the first project statement that turns the fuzzed chunk stream into the `coolkey_object_info` structure used by the vulnerable path.

tainted_value_origin.description: The first concrete vulnerability-relevant key parsed from attacker input is `object_id`. It is later passed back into the broken `coolkey_find_object_by_id()` lookup; the adjacent `object_len` parse at line 2166 separately supplies the 8447-byte allocation size seen by ASAN.

root_cause.description: Executed root cause on the witnessed path. `coolkey_fill_object()` assumes this lookup returns the list entry corresponding to `obj->id`, but the registered comparator is inverted for SimCList's `== 0` match contract, so the call can return a different list node. The next assignment then aliases one heap buffer into two objects.
root_cause.note: Later upstream fixes first flip the comparator and then add extra hardening checks (same-length validation and duplicate-ID rejection). The provided `patch.diff` only shows the final duplicate-ID guard, so it is not the sole causal evidence for this staged source.

sink.description: ASAN sink. During disconnect cleanup, the list walk frees `o->data` for every object entry; after the aliasing in `coolkey_fill_object()`, this line re-frees the same 8447-byte buffer from the second aliased node.
sink.note: The saved ASAN trace reports both the previous free and the crashing free at this line, with the same call chain `coolkey_free_private_data -> coolkey_finish -> sc_disconnect_card` and the allocation at `coolkey_fill_object:1401`.

parser_admitted.description: After applet selection and lifecycle reads succeed, `coolkey_initialize()` enters the LIST_OBJECTS enumeration loop and starts parsing attacker-controlled object descriptors from the staged chunk stream.

poc.trigger: The staged `poc` reproduces the saved AddressSanitizer double-free. It is a little-endian uint16 length-prefixed APDU-response stream whose early CoolKey LIST_OBJECTS replies create many placeholder objects, including numerous 8447-byte entries and additional different IDs. During PKCS#15 binding, `coolkey_find_object_by_template()` reaches `coolkey_fill_object()` for one 8447-byte candidate, and the inverted SimCList comparator lets `coolkey_find_object_by_id()` return another list node. `coolkey_fill_object()` then stores one heap allocation into both objects, and `sc_disconnect_card()` later frees that address twice.

format.name: length-prefixed CoolKey APDU-response stream
format.contract: The input is the harness's little-endian uint16 length-prefixed APDU-response stream. To preserve the witnessed trigger, the early chunks consumed by `COOLKEY_INS_LIST_OBJECTS` must leave `priv->objects_list` with at least one placeholder object whose parsed `length` is 8447 and at least one additional placeholder node with a different `id` and `data == NULL`; the staged witness does this with many 18-byte replies whose first 14 bytes include `20202020202020ff2020ff202020` and also distinct descriptors such as `62f4060020207aff202020ff2020`. Later chunks must still let `sc_pkcs15_bind()` reach `coolkey_find_object_by_template()` and final `sc_disconnect_card()` cleanup.

coarse_trace.summary: LIST_OBJECTS enumeration parses attacker-controlled object descriptors into persistent placeholder nodes in `priv->objects_list`, preserving both their IDs and lengths while leaving `data == NULL`.
PKCS#15 certificate matching iterates `priv->objects_list`, reaches a candidate object with `data == NULL`, and allocates its 8447-byte payload in `coolkey_fill_object()`.

The buggy ID lookup inside `coolkey_fill_object()` resolves the candidate against a different list element, and because the peer's `data` is still NULL, the same heap pointer is stored into both objects.
Disconnect cleanup walks the aliased list and frees `o->data` from one node and then again from the other, producing the ASAN double-free.

fine_trace.code: return coolkey_apdu_io(card, COOLKEY_CLASS, COOLKEY_INS_LIST_OBJECTS, seq, 0, NULL, 0, &rbuf, &rbuflen, NULL, 0);
fine_trace.note: LIST_OBJECTS copies one attacker-controlled reader-response chunk into `object_info`. Parsing the saved `poc` as the harness's little-endian uint16 chunk stream shows many early 18-byte replies whose first 14 bytes are `20 20 20 20 20 20 20 ff 20 20 ff 20 20 20`, plus distinct descriptors such as `62 f4 06 00 20 20 7a ff ...`; these are the exact bytes later parsed into object IDs and lengths.

Initialization parses the descriptor's `object_id` field into the list key. On the staged witness, early iterations yield repeated `object_id = 0x20202020` and other attacker-chosen IDs including `0x62f40600` and `0x202020ff`, so later lookups can encounter both same-ID and different-ID elements.

Initialization separately parses `object_length` and truncates the 32-bit big-endian value into `unsigned short object_len`. For the repeated `20 20 20 ff` descriptors this becomes `0x20ff = 8447`, the same allocation size AddressSanitizer later reports from `coolkey_fill_object:1401`.

Because these IDs are not the special combined-object ID `0x7a300000`, initialization takes the non-combined path and forwards each parsed `object_id` and `object_len` into placeholder-object creation while leaving `object_data` absent.

SimCList autocopy duplicates `new_object` into `priv->objects_list`, so each iteration leaves a persistent `sc_cardctl_coolkey_object_t` node with attacker-controlled `id`, attacker-controlled/truncated `length`, and `data == NULL`. After the early LIST_OBJECTS replies, the list contains many still-unfilled nodes, including 8447-byte entries and nodes with different IDs.

fine_trace.code: current = list_iterator_next(list); attribute.object = current; r = coolkey_find_attribute(card, &attribute);
fine_trace.note: During `sc_pkcs15_bind()`, `coolkey_find_matching_cert()` searches for a certificate with the current object's `CKA_ID`. `coolkey_find_object_by_template()` walks `priv->objects_list` and asks `coolkey_find_attribute()` to inspect each candidate. The ASAN allocation stack proves the crashing `coolkey_fill_object()` call enters through this iterator path, but the saved static artifacts do not identify which exact candidate node was selected.

For the selected candidate, `obj->data` is still NULL, so `coolkey_fill_object()` skips the early return and allocates `buf_len = obj->length` bytes. AddressSanitizer records the double-freed region as an 8447-byte allocation from this exact line, so the chosen candidate's cached length on the witnessed path is 8447.

Root cause. `coolkey_find_object_by_id()` delegates to `list_locate()`, which treats comparator result `0` as a match. But the registered `coolkey_compare_id()` returns `1` when IDs are equal and `0` when they differ. This call therefore resolves `obj->id` to the first non-equal list element rather than the intended matching entry whenever another ID exists. The saved artifacts do not identify that peer node precisely, only that it comes from `priv->objects_list` through this lookup.

On the witnessed path the misresolved peer's `data` field is still NULL, so this cleanup branch is not taken. If the guard were true, `coolkey_fill_object()` would free `new_obj_data` immediately and no shared ownership would be created.

The same heap pointer is written into both list elements: the current candidate `obj` and the different `obj_entry` returned by step 8. This creates shared ownership of one 8447-byte allocation inside `priv->objects_list`.

During `sc_disconnect_card()`, `coolkey_finish()` calls `coolkey_free_private_data()`, which iterates every list node and frees each `o->data`. When the loop reaches one of the aliased entries first, this `free()` releases the shared buffer and leaves the other node's `data` pointer dangling.

Sink. The same cleanup loop later reaches the second aliased node and executes `free(o->data)` on the already freed address. AddressSanitizer reports both the crash and previous free at this line, with the allocation at `coolkey_fill_object:1401`.

allocation_context.note: ASAN attributes the double-freed region to `malloc(buf_len)` here. The fine trace records the same executed allocation after `coolkey_find_object_by_template()` picks a candidate whose cached `length` is 8447.

free_context.note: The previous-free stack is identical to the crash stack at the application frames because the same cleanup loop reaches two different list nodes that now alias one `data` pointer.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: ASAN's 8447-byte region is allocated in `coolkey_fill_object` and then later double-freed in `coolkey_free_private_data`. The fine trace's root cause is the immediately following ID-lookup misuse at `coolkey_fill_object:1411`: because the comparator is inverted for SimCList's `== 0` contract, the fresh allocation can be attached to a second list node and later freed twice.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: The saved allocation stack matches fine-trace steps 6-12: `coolkey_find_matching_cert -> coolkey_find_object_by_template -> coolkey_find_attribute -> coolkey_fill_object` allocates the buffer, and `coolkey_free_private_data -> coolkey_finish -> sc_disconnect_card` later frees it twice. The static artifacts do not identify which exact peer node step 8 selected, so the trace keeps that peer abstract.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: The APDU stream controls the object IDs and cached lengths stored in `priv->objects_list`. Once the broken lookup in step 8 aliases `new_obj_data` into two list nodes, that attacker-derived `o->data` value is the same pointer that cleanup frees twice at the sink.
